patients.summary: Construction supervisor and heavy daily drinker who joined in 2022 with hypertension and asthma, was found to have acromegaly from a pituitary macroadenoma, then an ANCA vasculitis with kidney involvement. After his last practice visit in June 2024 the practice only receives records: alcohol pancreatitis, pituitary apoplexy with adrenal crisis, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with tumor lysis, and a shoulder dislocation with a cuff tear.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
50 y/o M here to establish. Construction supervisor, married.

He came in mostly because his hands and knees ache, worst first thing in the morning, going on about four months. Has had to take his wedding band off because it no longer goes past the knuckle, and he went up a size and a half in work boots this spring. Says his brother looked like this before he was diagnosed with acromegaly in his mid-forties, and his wife made him promise to mention it. No headaches or vision change he has noticed. Snores, unchanged.

PMH: hypertension for years on lisinopril 20 and HCTZ 25, home readings 'fine.' Asthma since he was a teenager, albuterol a few times a month, more with dust on site. No hospitalizations, no surgeries.
Alcohol: drinks every day, by his count 6 beers on a light night and closer to 12 on weekends, with some heavier stretches recently. Has never tried to quit, no withdrawal he recognizes, no DUIs. AUDIT-C 11. Never smoked. No drugs.
FHx: father HTN, stroke at 68. Mother autoimmune thyroid disease. Brother acromegaly, dx at 45.
NKDA.

Exam: big-framed man, coarse facial features with a prominent jaw. Teeth spaced. Hands broad and fleshy. Lungs clear, no wheeze. Heart regular, no murmur. Abdomen soft, no hepatomegaly. Knees bulky without effusion, full ROM. No edema. PHQ-9 3.

A/P
1. Acral enlargement, arthralgia, with a first-degree relative with acromegaly. This needs a proper look. Referred to endocrinology, asked them to see him soon.
2. HTN: near goal. Continue current meds. CMP today.
3. Alcohol use disorder, severe by history. We talked about what the beer is doing to his pressure and his liver and that cutting down is worth it on its own. Offered naltrexone 50 mg daily; he would rather try on his own first. Door left open.
4. Asthma, intermittent: albuterol only, fine.
5. Health maintenance: CBC, lipids, A1c, one-time HCV and HIV screens. FIT kit given. Records requested from prior office. Flu and COVID in the fall.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Keith, your labs from Tuesday look good: kidney function normal (creatinine 1.0), blood counts normal, liver tests and sugar in range, cholesterol acceptable. HIV and hepatitis C screens negative. Endocrinology should be calling you to schedule. Let me know if you haven't heard by the end of the month.

Reviewed and filed. - PCP

documents.title: Endocrinology consultation
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Outside endocrinology group
Date of visit: 9/5/2022
Reason for referral: possible acromegaly

Thank you for sending Mr. Bianchi, 50. He describes half a year of steadily worsening stiffness and pain in both knees and both hands, most noticeable on waking. His ring will no longer go on and his shoe size has gone up. His brother carries a diagnosis of acromegaly.

Medications: lisinopril 20 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, albuterol inhaler as needed. NKDA. Never smoker; drinks heavily on a daily basis. Construction supervisor.

BP 140/85, HR 78.
Exam: prognathic jaw and macroglossia. Soft-tissue thickening of both hands. Knees with bony enlargement, range of motion preserved.

Results: IGF-1 elevated for age. Random GH elevated. On a 75 g oral glucose load GH failed to suppress.
Hand and knee radiographs: widened joint spaces, no significant osteophytes.

Impression: acromegaly, biochemically confirmed.
Plan: dedicated pituitary MRI. Visual fields if the adenoma approaches the chiasm. Will see him back with imaging to discuss treatment.

Allergies: NKDA

reports.study: MRI pituitary with and without contrast
reports.text:
Indication: acromegaly.
Technique: thin-section sagittal and coronal T1 and T2 imaging through the sella before and after gadolinium, dynamic coronal post-contrast series.
Findings: 1.8 cm sellar mass enhancing less than the normal gland, with mild suprasellar extension. The optic chiasm sits above the mass without compression. Cavernous sinuses unremarkable. No hemorrhage. Brain parenchyma otherwise unremarkable.
reports.conclusion: 1.8 cm sellar mass with mild suprasellar extension, chiasm not compressed, consistent with pituitary macroadenoma.

documents.title: MRI reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Pituitary MRI reviewed: 1.8 cm macroadenoma, chiasm clear. Fits the endocrine picture. Endocrinology letter arrived today too. They will go over treatment with him. Portal note sent to pt.

documents.title: Endocrinology follow-up
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Outside endocrinology group
Date of visit: 11/8/2022

Follow-up for acromegaly. MRI 9/16 showed a 1.8 cm macroadenoma with mild suprasellar extension, chiasm clear. He saw neurosurgery on 10/20, who recommended transsphenoidal resection. He has declined surgery for now; he does not want time off work and is uneasy about an operation. We discussed that surgery offers the best chance of cure, and that medical therapy controls GH in many patients but rarely shrinks the tumor away.

Plan: octreotide LAR 20 mg IM every 4 weeks starting today, first dose given in clinic. Gallbladder symptoms reviewed. IGF-1 in 3 months to titrate. Revisit surgery at each visit.

Medications: lisinopril 20 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg, albuterol as needed, octreotide LAR as above. NKDA.

Faxed at the request of the primary care office.

S: About 10 days of stuffy nose, thick discharge, pressure over the cheeks and forehead, worse bending over. Thought it was a cold, not getting better. No fever. Mild cough. Using albuterol a little more.
Also tells me he has been getting a monthly shot at endocrinology since November for the pituitary tumor. We had not received a note about that; added octreotide LAR to his list and asked the front desk to request the visit note. He saw neurosurgery and doesn't want surgery right now.

O: Afebrile. Maxillary and frontal tenderness. Turbinates swollen, purulent drainage. TMs clear. Lungs with no wheeze today. 

A/P: Sinusitis, past the window where it usually clears on its own. Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 twice a day x 10 days, saline rinses. Call if not improving. BP 140s, recheck at next visit.
Octreotide noted, endocrine to manage.

orders.reason: bilateral nodular infiltrates, hemoptysis, weight loss

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Sinuses never cleared after two antibiotic courses, going on close to two months now. Cough brings up phlegm and a few times there have been streaks of blood. Down about 10 lb since July without trying. Feels run down, and his joints are aching in a different way than before, more all over. No fever he has measured. No rash.

O: Weight 99.5 kg (104 in July). Afebrile, sats normal on room air. Nasal mucosa crusted. Scattered expiratory wheeze both sides. Heart regular. No rash, no lymphadenopathy.
CXR in office: multiple nodular opacities in both lungs.

A/P: Refractory sinus disease, hemoptysis, weight loss, joint aches and bilateral lung nodules. Worried about a systemic process (vasculitis, infection, malignancy all on the list). Called pulmonology directly, they will see him 3/8. Told him to go to the ED for anything more than streaks of blood or for shortness of breath. Holding off on more antibiotics.

conditions.label: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis with renal involvement

documents.title: Pulmonology consultation
documents.author: pulmonology
documents.body:
Outside pulmonary group
Visit date: 3/8/2023
Referred for: bilateral lung nodules

50 year old man with acromegaly from a pituitary macroadenoma, on octreotide since November, who has had sinus symptoms since early January that did not respond to two courses of antibiotics. Over the same stretch, a productive cough with intermittent small-volume hemoptysis, about 10 lb of weight loss, general malaise, and joint pains that are new and separate from his acromegalic arthropathy.

Meds per patient: lisinopril, HCTZ, albuterol as needed, octreotide LAR. NKDA. Never smoker. Heavy daily alcohol.

Exam: afebrile. BP 145/90. Diffuse wheezes throughout both lung fields. Skin without rash.

Data: chest radiograph from his PCP 2/23 reviewed, bilateral nodular infiltrates. Urinalysis today: blood 2+, red blood cell casts on microscopy. Creatinine 2.8, up from 1.0 last year. Normocytic anemia, hemoglobin 11.2. ESR 72.

Impression: upper airway disease, pulmonary nodules with hemoptysis and an active urinary sediment with rising creatinine. This picture is granulomatosis with polyangiitis until proven otherwise, with renal involvement.

Plan: ANCA serologies sent. Urgent rheumatology referral, which I have arranged for next week; they will direct induction therapy and involve nephrology as needed. CT chest at their discretion. He knows to go to the ED for heavier bleeding or breathlessness.

documents.title: Call with patient
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Pulmonology called me yesterday afternoon with their impression. Called Keith on his lunch. Explained GPA in plain terms, that the kidneys are involved and that treatment is usually steroids plus an infusion drug, and that it generally works. Rheumatology appointment 3/14 confirmed. Asked him to hold off on ibuprofen and to drink less, ideally none, given the kidneys. He was quiet but asked good questions. Will see him after rheumatology starts treatment.

medications.sig: Take 3 tablets (60 mg) by mouth daily, then taper per rheumatology
IV infusion at the rheumatology infusion center per rheumatology (induction 375 mg/m2 weekly x4, then maintenance)

medications.drug: sulfamethoxazole 800 MG / trimethoprim 160 MG Oral Tablet
medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth three times weekly (Mon, Wed, Fri)

documents.title: Rheumatology consultation
documents.author: rheumatology
documents.body:
Outside rheumatology practice
Seen 3/14/2023

Assessment: ANCA-associated vasculitis, clinically granulomatosis with polyangiitis, with sinus, pulmonary (nodules, hemoptysis) and renal (RBC casts, creatinine 2.8) involvement. Organ-threatening disease.

Plan:
- Prednisone 60 mg daily, taper over roughly 5 to 6 months per the schedule given to him.
- Rituximab 375 mg/m2 IV weekly x 4, first infusion this week.
- Hepatitis B surface antigen negative and hepatitis C antibody negative today, cleared for rituximab.
- TMP-SMX DS three times a week for PJP prophylaxis while on prednisone.
- Weekly BMP and CBC for the first month, then with PCP visits.
- Discussed alcohol and steroids, bone and stomach protection, and infection precautions. He was advised to hold off on live vaccines.

Current medications: lisinopril 20 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, albuterol as needed, octreotide LAR 20 mg monthly, plus the above. NKDA.

documents.title: Infusion scheduling
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Rheumatology infusion nurse called to confirm our office has no conflicting orders and to ask for his last CBC. Faxed 3/8 pulmonology labs. First rituximab infusion tomorrow.

documents.title: Can't sleep
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Is it normal to be wide awake at 2am on this prednisone? Also hungry all the time. Wife says I'm short with everybody.

documents.title: RE: Can't sleep
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Very normal at 60 mg, unfortunately. Take the whole dose first thing in the morning, not later in the day. It gets better as the dose comes down. If the moods get to be more than irritability, call me. And the alcohol makes all of this harder, sleep included.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Follow-up GPA. Four rituximab infusions done. Prednisone now 40 mg on the taper sheet.
Sinuses much better, cough nearly gone, no blood since mid-March. Joints less achy. Sleep still poor. Drinking 'less', he says maybe 4 to 6 a night.

BP 142/88, afebrile. Nasal crusting improved. Lungs clear today. Moon face starting. No edema.

Labs today: creatinine 1.9 (2.8 at diagnosis), hemoglobin 11.9, UA still 1+ blood.

A/P:
- GPA with renal involvement, responding. Rheumatology following; copied them on labs.
- Sinusitis label closed, this was the vasculitis.
- HTN slightly above goal on prednisone, no change yet.
- PCV20 today given immunosuppression and alcohol use.
- Alcohol: acknowledged the cutback, encouraged more. Still not interested in medication.
RTC 2 months.

documents.title: Labs from today
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Keith, your kidney number came down from 2.8 to 1.9, which is real progress, and your blood count is starting to recover. Rheumatology has the results. Keep the TMP-SMX going three days a week.

documents.title: Refill request

reports.text:
Specimen: kidney, left, percutaneous needle core biopsy.
Light microscopy: glomeruli with segmental fibrinoid necrosis and cellular crescents. Interstitial inflammation in the surrounding cortex.
Immunofluorescence: no significant immunoglobulin or complement deposition (pauci-immune pattern).
Electron microscopy: no immune-type electron-dense deposits.
reports.conclusion: Pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis, consistent with ANCA-associated vasculitis.

documents.title: Emergency department record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital ED, 10/27/2023

51 M with granulomatosis with polyangiitis, in remission over the summer and off steroids since early September, presenting with two weeks of tiredness and passing less urine, swelling in both legs that is new, and three days of urine the color of cola. No sinus congestion, earache or rash.

BP 155/95. Crackles at both bases. 2+ pitting edema of both legs to the knee.

UA: protein 2+, blood 3+, >50 RBC/hpf. Creatinine 4.6. CRP 46. p-ANCA positive by immunofluorescence.

Impression: rapidly progressive renal failure in a patient with known ANCA vasculitis, likely relapse.
Plan: admit to nephrology. Kidney biopsy. Hold lisinopril and HCTZ. Rheumatology aware.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
Regional hospital, admitted 10/27/2023, discharged 11/3/2023

Principal diagnosis: microscopic polyangiitis (p-ANCA positive) with pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis; acute kidney injury.
History: ANCA-associated vasculitis first diagnosed as GPA 3/2023 (sinus, lung nodules, renal), induced with prednisone and rituximab, prednisone completed 9/2023.

Course: Creatinine 4.6 on arrival. Renal biopsy 10/30: pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic GN. Rheumatology and nephrology agree on microscopic polyangiitis features alongside his prior GPA picture. Methylprednisolone 500 mg IV daily x 3, then prednisone 60 mg daily. Rituximab 1 g IV 10/31; second dose due day 15 at the outpatient infusion center. IV furosemide for volume overload with good diuresis; edema and crackles improved. Did not require dialysis. Lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide held. Creatinine 3.4 at discharge.

Discharge medications: prednisone 60 mg daily with taper per rheumatology; TMP-SMX DS three times weekly; albuterol as needed; octreotide LAR per endocrinology. HOLD lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide until reviewed by nephrology.
Allergies: NKDA
Follow-up: PCP within 1 week, nephrology 4 to 6 weeks, rheumatology 2 weeks.

documents.title: Hospital records reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Discharge summary, ED note and biopsy report received and reviewed. Matches what we went over on 11/9. Problem list updated with MPA; GPA left on as rheumatology still carries both labels. Lisinopril and HCTZ remain on hold pending nephrology.

documents.title: In the hospital
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Wanted you to know I've been in the hospital since Friday. Kidneys went bad again, legs blew up. They did a biopsy this morning. Back on the big steroid dose. They say maybe home end of the week.

documents.title: RE: In the hospital
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Thanks for telling me, Keith, I'm sorry this flared. I'll ask the hospital for records. When you're discharged, call us and we'll get you in within the week so we can go over everything and check labs.

documents.title: Records request
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Pt discharged Friday. Requested discharge summary, ED note and biopsy report from hospital HIM by fax. TCM visit booked 11/9 at 4:30.

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Hospital follow-up. Admitted 10/27 to 11/3 with a vasculitis relapse in the kidneys. Hospital summary not here yet; going off his discharge paperwork and what he tells me. Biopsy showed crescentic GN, pauci-immune. p-ANCA positive. Got 3 days of IV steroids and the first of two rituximab doses, second scheduled at the infusion center next week. Discharge creatinine 3.4 per the paperwork.

Feels washed out. Urine looks normal color now. Leg swelling down a lot. Took the water pill in the hospital, none since. Lisinopril and HCTZ both on hold per the hospital. Prednisone 60 mg. TMP-SMX back on. Says he hasn't had a drink since the admission.

BP 152/94 off both BP meds. Lungs clear. Trace ankle edema. 
Labs today: creatinine 2.6, Hgb 12.1, UA blood 2+, protein 1+.

A/P:
- Microscopic polyangiitis / GPA relapse with crescentic GN and AKI. Creatinine trending down. Rituximab dose 2 next week. Rheumatology and nephrology appointments made.
- HTN: elevated off meds and on high-dose prednisone. Leaving them held as the hospital asked until nephrology sees him; he'll check home BP daily and send readings. Low salt.
- Alcohol: congratulated him on two weeks without. Offered support again.
- Med list reconciled. Records request sent again for the summary.

documents.title: Records request, second
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: No records yet from the hospital. Called HIM, they had no request on file. Sent the request again with the signed release. They said 3 to 5 business days.

documents.title: Nephrology follow-up
documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
Outside nephrology group
Visit 12/12/2023

Follow-up after admission for p-ANCA crescentic GN. Both rituximab doses received. Prednisone tapering per rheumatology, currently 40 mg. Edema resolved. Home BP readings 140s to 150s over 90s.
Creatinine today 1.9 (3.4 at discharge). 
Plan: restart lisinopril 20 mg daily for blood pressure and antiproteinuric effect; BMP in 2 weeks with PCP. Hydrochlorothiazide stays off for now, PCP may resume if BP remains above goal. Return 3 months.
NKDA.

documents.title: Nephrology note reviewed

documents.body: Thanks. Potassium and kidney function were fine on the December draw. Your numbers are still above where I want them. Let's look at adding back the HCTZ when I see you in February, once the prednisone is lower. Keep logging.

documents.author: PCP

Back on lisinopril since December. Prednisone down to 10 mg. Feels stronger, working full days. Admits to a few beers on weekends again, 'not like before.'

BP 146/90, home log similar. No edema. Lungs clear. Steroid fullness in the face easing.
Creatinine 1.5 today, UA clean.

- MPA/GPA: in remission per rheum. Maintenance rituximab due in April.
- Alcohol: back to some drinking. Reminded him what the kidneys and the vasculitis have been through. He hears it.
RTC 3 months.

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Rescheduled from April. He has been dragging for a couple of months, tired by midafternoon and asleep in the chair after dinner. Less interest in sex, his words, which his wife has noticed. Pants tighter. Finished prednisone mid-May. Rituximab maintenance in April. Monthly octreotide shots continuing. No headaches or vision change. No sinus, cough or blood in urine.
Drinking is back to most nights, 6 or more. AUDIT-C 12. Naltrexone offered again, declined. PHQ-9 4, doesn't feel depressed, just tired.

O: BP 134/84, weight 107 kg (103 last summer). Lungs clear. No edema. No rash.
Labs today: creatinine 1.2, Hgb 13.8, rest of CMP fine.

A/P:
1. Fatigue, low libido, weight gain. Coming off months of steroids and drinking nightly, both can do this. Not starting anything today. He sees endocrinology for the octreotide every month; asked him to bring these symptoms up there next visit. 
2. HTN at goal on lisinopril and HCTZ.
3. ANCA vasculitis in remission, kidney function back near baseline. AKI resolved. Prednisone and TMP-SMX off the list.
4. Alcohol use disorder, severe, ongoing. Brief counseling again.
RTC 3 to 4 months, physical in the fall.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Keith, kidney function is the best it has been since all this started (creatinine 1.2), and the blood count is back to normal. Liver and sugar fine. Please do mention the tiredness and the libido to endocrinology when you go for your shot this month.

reports.text: Gallbladder without stones or wall thickening. Common bile duct not dilated; no intrahepatic biliary dilation. Pancreas partly obscured by bowel gas. Liver normal in size. Kidneys normal in size without hydronephrosis. Spleen normal.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Regional hospital. Admitted 7/2/2024, discharged 7/19/2024.

Principal diagnosis: severe acute pancreatitis, alcohol-induced, with organ failure.
Secondary: acute kidney injury; ANCA vasculitis in remission; acromegaly; hypertension; asthma; alcohol use disorder.

Presentation: one day of intense upper abdominal pain boring through to the back, with nausea and repeated vomiting, after a week of very heavy drinking. Febrile 38.3, HR 110, RR 22, BP 90/60. Abdomen distended and tender throughout with quiet bowel sounds.
Labs: WBC 16.0, Hct 48, BUN 36, amylase 1200, lipase 2500, calcium 7.8, CRP 150.
Ultrasound: no gallstones, no biliary dilation.

Course: Over the first two days he became more unwell despite aggressive IV fluids, with ongoing hypotension, low urine output and a climbing oxygen requirement. Transferred to the ICU: norepinephrine for blood pressure support, heated high-flow oxygen, continued fluids. No dialysis needed; urine output and creatinine recovered over the following week. Weaned off pressors and oxygen, diet advanced.

Alcohol: counseled on complete abstinence; he states he plans to stop.
Discharge medications: lisinopril 20 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, albuterol as needed, octreotide LAR per endocrinology.
Allergies: NKDA
Follow-up: PCP 1 to 2 weeks.

events.reason: sudden severe headache, blurred vision, confusion

reports.text:
Indication: thunderclap headache, ophthalmoplegia, known pituitary macroadenoma.
The sellar mass is larger than on the prior study, with signal consistent with recent hemorrhage within it. Ventricles normal in size. No other intracranial hemorrhage. No acute infarct.
reports.conclusion: Enlarged sellar mass with recent hemorrhage, consistent with pituitary apoplexy.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: intensive care
documents.body:
Regional hospital. Admitted 1/9/2025 through the ED to the ICU; discharged 1/17/2025.

Diagnoses: pituitary apoplexy (hemorrhage into known macroadenoma) with secondary adrenal insufficiency presenting as adrenal crisis.
Background: acromegaly on octreotide LAR, ANCA vasculitis (GPA/MPA) on rituximab maintenance, severe alcohol pancreatitis 7/2024, hypertension, asthma, alcohol use disorder. Before this admission he had been worked up elsewhere for fatigue, reduced libido and some weight gain without any treatment started.

Presentation: abrupt onset of the worst headache he has had, with nausea and blurry vision. His wife found him muddled and struggling to name everyday things. No anticoagulant use.
T 36.8, BP 88/54, HR 118, RR 22. Sweaty and agitated. Both eyelids drooping, eye movements limited, peripheral vision reduced to confrontation. Heart and lungs normal.
Labs: mild hyponatremia, hypoglycemia.
MRI: enlarged sellar mass with recent hemorrhage.

Course: stress-dose IV hydrocortisone and fluids with prompt rise in blood pressure, correction of sodium and glucose, and clearing of confusion. Neurosurgery and endocrinology followed; with steady improvement in eye movements and vision, managed without surgery. Ptosis and eye movement improving at discharge. Octreotide continued.

Discharge medications: hydrocortisone 15 mg each morning and 5 mg mid-afternoon (double for fever or illness, emergency injection kit, medical alert ID advised); lisinopril 20 mg daily; hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; albuterol as needed; octreotide LAR monthly.
Allergies: NKDA
Follow-up: endocrinology 2 weeks, neuro-ophthalmology, PCP.

documents.title: Hospital records reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Discharge summary for the January ICU stay received and reviewed: pituitary apoplexy with adrenal crisis, managed without surgery, discharged on hydrocortisone via endocrinology. Pt has not been in since last June. Filed; will reconcile when he comes in.

documents.title: Refill request, hydrocortisone
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Pharmacy sent refill request for hydrocortisone 10 mg and 5 mg tablets, original prescriber a hospital physician. Not on our med list. Routed to PCP.

documents.title: Call with patient
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Per PCP called pt about hydrocortisone. He says he was in the ICU last month, bleed into the pituitary tumor, now on hydrocortisone for life. Taking 15 mg morning and 5 mg mid-afternoon. Has an endocrinology visit Thursday. Advised him to have endocrinology take over the prescription and confirmed he has enough until then (about 10 days). Reviewed doubling dose if sick and going to the ED if vomiting and can't keep it down. Records request sent to hospital. Pt said he would schedule with us but did not want to set a date today.

documents.title: Refill request
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Lisinopril and HCTZ refilled x 90 days. Hospital summary from January reviewed (apoplexy, adrenal insufficiency, hydrocortisone via endocrinology). Has not been seen since last June despite outreach. Front desk to try again.

documents.title: News
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Figured I should tell you. They found a lymphoma last week, the oncologist called it high grade B cell. Chemo is supposed to start Saturday. I know I owe you a visit.

documents.title: RE: News
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Keith, thank you for telling me. I'm sorry. You don't owe me anything, but I'd like to stay in the loop. Please ask the oncology office to copy me on their notes. Keep taking your hydrocortisone, and remember to double it if you get sick during chemo. Message me any time.

reports.text: Sinus rhythm, rate 96. Normal axis. Peaked T waves in the precordial leads. No ST elevation.
reports.conclusion: Peaked T waves, consistent with hyperkalemia.

documents.title: Emergency department record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital ED, 7/3/2025

53 year old man with acromegaly from a pituitary macroadenoma, apoplexy in January now on hydrocortisone, ANCA vasculitis (GPA/MPA), prior alcohol pancreatitis, and alcohol use disorder. High-grade B-cell lymphoma diagnosed a week ago; first chemotherapy planned in two days. Here with nausea, vomiting and lethargy. Denies fever, cough or diarrhea.

BP 145/90, HR 98. Awake and oriented but fatigued. No palpable lymph nodes, no liver or spleen enlargement.
Na 138, K 6.5, Cl 100, HCO3 22, BUN 28, creatinine 2.1 (baseline 1.0), uric acid 12, calcium 7.8, phosphorus 6.5.
ECG: peaked T waves.

Impression: spontaneous tumor lysis syndrome with hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury before chemotherapy.
Treatment: IV calcium gluconate, IV insulin with dextrose, rasburicase, IV fluids; stress-dose hydrocortisone given. Oncology consulted; admitted to the oncology service. Chemotherapy to be postponed until kidney function and electrolytes recover.
Allergies: NKDA

documents.title: ED record reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: ED record 7/3 reviewed: spontaneous tumor lysis before first chemo, K 6.5, creatinine 2.1, admitted to oncology. No inpatient summary yet. Chemo postponed per ED note.

reports.text: Sinus rhythm, rate 98. Peaked T waves. Intervals normal.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: hematology/oncology
documents.body:
Regional hospital. Admitted 8/9/2025 (ICU), discharged 8/14/2025.

Diagnosis: tumor lysis syndrome after cycle 1 of R-CHOP for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma; acute kidney injury; hyperkalemia.
History: DLBCL diagnosed 6/2025; spontaneous tumor lysis 7/2025 delayed treatment. Cycle 1 R-CHOP given 8/7 with allopurinol and IV hydration. Also acromegaly, secondary adrenal insufficiency after pituitary apoplexy on hydrocortisone, ANCA vasculitis, prior pancreatitis, hypertension, asthma, alcohol use disorder.

Presentation, 48 hours after cycle 1: nausea, vomiting, lethargy and muscle cramping. Tired-appearing. T 37.2, BP 130/85, HR 98, RR 18. Mildly tender in both flanks.
Na 138, K 6.2, Cl 100, HCO3 22, BUN 28, creatinine 2.1 (baseline 0.9), calcium 7.2, phosphorus 6.5, uric acid 12. ECG with peaked T waves.

Course: ICU for cardiac monitoring. IV calcium gluconate, insulin with dextrose, rasburicase, aggressive IV fluids; stress-dose hydrocortisone. Potassium and phosphorus normalized over 72 hours, creatinine improving. No dialysis.
Discharge medications: allopurinol 300 mg daily through cycle 2; hydrocortisone 15 mg AM / 5 mg afternoon; lisinopril 20 mg daily; hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; albuterol as needed.
Allergies: NKDA
Follow-up: oncology clinic in 1 week; cycle 2 planned on schedule with TLS precautions.

documents.title: Records request

documents.title: Refill request

documents.title: Done with chemo
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Finished my 6th round of R-CHOP on November 20. Had the PET scan last Thursday and the oncologist says there's no active cancer left, complete response. Thought you'd want to know some good news for a change.

documents.title: RE: Done with chemo
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: That is wonderful news, Keith, thank you for sharing it. Please ask oncology to send me the PET report and their summary. When you're up for it after the holidays, come in so we can catch up on everything from this past year.

events.reason: right shoulder injury after fall from ladder

reports.text: Right shoulder, AP and axillary views. The humeral head is displaced anteriorly and inferiorly relative to the glenoid. No fracture of the humeral head, greater tuberosity or glenoid rim identified.
Right shoulder, post-reduction AP and axillary views. Humeral head now congruent with the glenoid. No fracture.

documents.title: Emergency department record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital ED, 3/14/2026

53 M with acromegaly, ANCA vasculitis, adrenal insufficiency on hydrocortisone, and DLBCL recently completing chemotherapy. Came off a ladder and landed directly on the right shoulder, with pain right away. 

Exam on arrival: right shoulder contour squared off, acromion prominent, tender anteriorly. Distal sensation and pulses intact.
X-ray: anterior dislocation, no fracture.

Procedural sedation and closed reduction by orthopedics, uncomplicated. Post-reduction film reduced, no fracture.
After reduction he still could not lift the arm out to the side past about 30 degrees and was weak resisting external rotation; sensation normal throughout the arm.
Impression: anterior shoulder dislocation, reduced; suspected rotator cuff tear.
Plan: sling, ice, analgesia; he was told to take his extra hydrocortisone dose today. Orthopedics clinic within 2 weeks for MRI.
Allergies: NKDA. Medications per patient: lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, albuterol, hydrocortisone.

documents.title: Your shoulder
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Keith, I just saw the ED record from the 14th. Sorry about the fall. Make sure you get the orthopedic follow-up and MRI they mentioned, and keep taking the extra hydrocortisone if the pain spikes or you feel unwell. Let me know how you're doing.

documents.title: Orthopedics follow-up
documents.author: orthopedics
documents.body:
Outside orthopedic group
Seen 4/2/2026

Right shoulder 3 weeks after anterior dislocation, reduced in the ED. Still weak lifting the arm overhead. Active abduction limited, passive range better. External rotation strength reduced.
MRI right shoulder: full-thickness tear of the supraspinatus tendon. Glenohumeral joint located.
Assessment: right full-thickness supraspinatus tear after anterior dislocation.
Plan: physical therapy twice weekly for 6 to 8 weeks; if strength and function do not come back, arthroscopic repair would be discussed. He prefers to try therapy first. Return 8 weeks.
NKDA.

documents.title: Orthopedics note reviewed

documents.body: Ortho letter: full-thickness supraspinatus tear on MRI, PT first. Filed.

documents.title: Shoulder and refills

documents.body: Shoulder is coming along with PT, still can't get it all the way up. Can you send my blood pressure pills again? I'll call about coming in once things slow down at work.

documents.title: RE: Shoulder and refills
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Glad PT is helping. I sent 30 days of both. I really do need to see you and check your kidney numbers before another refill. It's been almost two years and a lot has happened. Please book anything in the next month.
